newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong seen following U.S. rates higher.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong seen following U.S. rates higher.

text.p: Hong Kong is expected to follow the United States and jack up short-term interest rates, partly in an attempt to cool the red hot property sector, economists said on Wednesday.
"The conditions in Hong Kong seem to be that they need to follow," said George Leung, economic adviser at Hongkong Bank.
"(Higher rates) will affect mortgage rates, and that will have an impact to cool down the property market," he said.

In Hong Kong's small and quirky interest rate world, the Hong Kong Association of Banks regulates short-term deposit rates that quickly influence unregulated administrative rates such as mortgage and prime rates.

At a special meeting set for Wednesday at 4.30 p.m. (0830 GMT), the Hong Kong Association of Banks was expected to raise short-term deposit rates following the U.S. Federal Reserve's 25-basis point hike in the fed funds rate to 5.50 percent.

The HKAB meeting follows further signs of overheating in the property sector. Frenzied bidding at a land auction on Tuesday lifted the price of a 25,592 square metre plot in Chai Wan to a record HK$11.82 billion (US$1.53 billion) from an opening bid of HK$6.3 billion (US$800 million).
Speculation is now rife that a Wednesday meeting between the government and the Property Developers Association will generate a set of measures to cool down the sector.
Domestic issues rather than risk premiums would drive any rate increase by the Hong Kong Association of Banks, said Ian Perkin, Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce chief economist.

"If the bankers association is to move and lift the prime rate in Hong Kong, I would think it would be aimed more at domestic policy matters, that is, the overheated property, the buoyant share market, rather than following the rate itself," Perkin told Radio Television Hong Kong on Wednesday.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, raised its Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) rates by 25 basis points earlier Wednesday to between 4.25 percent and 6.25 percent from 4.0 percent and 6.0 percent.
The LAF is used by the HKMA to regulate short-term government rates and keep the Hong Kong dollar pegged at about HK$7.80 to the U.S. dollar.

Short-term Hong Kong government paper already trades at a premium to U.S. paper, with the spread between Hong Kong's three-month Exchange Fund Note and the three-month U.S. treasury a negative 20 basis points.
"This is more a feature of Hong Kong conditions, market conditions," Leung said. "There's more liquidity in the system."
Further along the curve, the spreads become positive, with the spread between the two-year EFN and the two-year U.S. treasury a positive 18 points.
Leung also said Hong Kong banks have little room left to manoeuvre on net interest margins, which have narrowed following an intense mortgage price war.
"Banks have faced severe competition, so if Hong Kong does not follow, there will be further pressure on Hong Kong banks' net interest margins," he said.
